title: Cascaded Denoising Diffusion for High-Resolution Image Synthesis
abstract: We present a cascaded denoising diffusion model that generates 1024px images by chaining a base generator with two diffusion super-resolution stages. Noise conditioning augmentation keeps the stages robust to their own sampling errors.
method: Each stage is a U-Net trained with the epsilon-prediction objective on a cosine noise schedule. The super-resolution stages receive the low-resolution image corrupted by Gaussian noise of a random level and learn to ignore its artifacts.
table:
| Model | FID (ImageNet 256) | Sampling steps |
| Cascaded diffusion (ours) | 3.52 | 250 |
| BigGAN-deep | 6.95 | 1 |
| Single-stage diffusion | 10.94 | 250 |
conclusion: Cascading lets each diffusion stage specialise and lowers FID by more than half against a single-stage baseline.

title: Latent Diffusion with Learned Autoencoders for Efficient Image Generation
abstract: Running the denoising diffusion process in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder cuts training compute while keeping image fidelity. We study the trade-off between latent compression and sample quality.
method: A KL-regularised autoencoder compresses images by a factor of 8. The diffusion U-Net operates on the 32x32 latent grid with cross-attention for text conditioning.
table:
| Model | FID (COCO captions) | GPU days |
| Latent diffusion (ours) | 7.81 | 79 |
| Pixel diffusion | 8.21 | 340 |
| Autoregressive transformer | 12.30 | 290 |
conclusion: Latent diffusion reaches better FID at roughly a quarter of the compute of pixel-space diffusion.

title: Consistency Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion Sampling
abstract: Diffusion models need hundreds of network evaluations per image. We distill a pretrained diffusion teacher into a consistency student that maps any noisy point on the trajectory to the clean image in one to four steps.
method: The student is trained to agree with itself across adjacent timesteps of the teacher's probability-flow ODE. An exponential moving average target stabilises training.
table:
| Sampler | FID (CIFAR-10) | Steps |
| Consistency student (ours) | 3.55 | 2 |
| DDIM | 4.67 | 50 |
| Progressive distillation | 5.58 | 2 |
conclusion: Two-step consistency sampling matches the quality of fifty-step DDIM.

title: Classifier-Free Guidance Schedules for Text-to-Image Diffusion
abstract: Classifier-free guidance trades diversity for prompt alignment in text-to-image diffusion. We show that a guidance weight that rises over the denoising trajectory improves both CLIP score and FID.
method: We parameterise the guidance weight as a monotone function of the noise level and search its shape on a held-out prompt set. No retraining of the diffusion model is needed.
table:
| Guidance | FID (COCO) | CLIP score |
| Rising schedule (ours) | 9.12 | 0.318 |
| Constant w=7.5 | 11.40 | 0.312 |
| No guidance | 18.75 | 0.271 |
conclusion: A rising guidance schedule is a free improvement for any text-to-image diffusion sampler.

title: Score-Based Generative Modeling with Variance-Preserving SDEs
abstract: We revisit score-based generative models through stochastic differential equations and show that a variance-preserving SDE with a predictor-corrector sampler sets a new likelihood record on image benchmarks.
method: A noise-conditional score network is trained with denoising score matching across a continuum of noise scales. Sampling alternates a reverse-SDE predictor with Langevin corrector steps.
table:
| Model | NLL (bits/dim, CIFAR-10) | FID |
| VP-SDE (ours) | 2.99 | 2.92 |
| DDPM | 3.70 | 3.17 |
| Glow | 3.35 | 48.90 |
conclusion: Treating denoising diffusion as an SDE unifies sampling and likelihood evaluation.

title: Message Passing Neural Networks for Quantum Chemistry Property Prediction
abstract: We frame molecular property prediction as message passing on the molecular graph, where atoms are nodes and bonds are edges, and predict DFT-level energies on the QM9 benchmark.
method: Edge networks compute messages from bond features; a gated recurrent unit updates atom states for six rounds and a set2set readout produces the molecule embedding.
table:
| Model | QM9 U0 MAE (meV) | Params |
| MPNN (ours) | 19.4 | 2.1M |
| SchNet | 14.0 | 1.8M |
| Kernel ridge regression | 128.0 | - |
conclusion: Learned message passing replaces hand-crafted molecular descriptors.

title: Equivariant Graph Networks for Molecular Dynamics Force Fields
abstract: E(3)-equivariant graph neural networks predict forces that rotate with the molecule. We build an equivariant force field that is data efficient on small organic molecules.
method: Node features carry irreducible representations up to degree two; tensor-product convolutions over a radius graph keep every layer equivariant.
table:
| Model | MD17 aspirin force MAE (meV/A) | Training samples |
| Equivariant GNN (ours) | 8.5 | 1000 |
| SchNet | 58.5 | 1000 |
| DimeNet | 21.6 | 1000 |
conclusion: Equivariance cuts force error several times at the same data budget.

title: Self-Supervised Pretraining of Graph Neural Networks on Ten Million Molecules
abstract: We pretrain a graph neural network on ten million unlabeled molecules with masked atom prediction and graph-level contrastive learning, then fine-tune on MoleculeNet property tasks.
method: Masked atom prediction recovers atom types from their neighbourhood; the contrastive objective aligns two augmented views of each molecular graph.
table:
| Model | BBBP ROC-AUC | Tox21 ROC-AUC |
| Pretrained GIN (ours) | 72.6 | 78.1 |
| GIN from scratch | 65.8 | 74.0 |
| Fingerprint + MLP | 68.0 | 72.9 |
conclusion: Pretraining on unlabeled molecules gives consistent gains on low-data property benchmarks.

title: Directed Message Passing for Drug Toxicity Prediction
abstract: Directed bond-level message passing on molecular graphs avoids the totters that undirected node-level passing suffers from. We apply it to toxicity endpoints used in early drug discovery.
method: Hidden states live on directed bonds; a message from bond u-v excludes the reverse bond v-u. Molecular descriptors are concatenated before the readout layer.
table:
| Model | ClinTox ROC-AUC | SIDER ROC-AUC |
| D-MPNN (ours) | 89.7 | 64.6 |
| Random forest | 76.3 | 63.8 |
| GCN | 80.7 | 59.4 |
conclusion: Bond-level message passing is a strong default for molecular toxicity prediction.

title: Graph Transformers for Molecular Property Regression
abstract: Global attention over all atom pairs, with shortest-path and 3D distance encodings, lets a graph transformer outperform local message passing on the PCQM4Mv2 HOMO-LUMO gap task.
method: Attention biases encode the shortest-path distance between atoms and a Gaussian expansion of their 3D distance; a virtual node aggregates the molecule.
table:
| Model | PCQM4Mv2 valid MAE (eV) | Layers |
| Graph transformer (ours) | 0.0864 | 12 |
| GIN-virtual | 0.1083 | 5 |
| GCN | 0.1379 | 5 |
conclusion: Structural encodings make attention competitive on molecular graphs.

title: Conformer Encoders for End-to-End Speech Recognition
abstract: Combining convolution and self-attention in each encoder block captures both local and global acoustic context. Our conformer transducer improves word error rate on LibriSpeech.
method: Each block sandwiches a multi-head self-attention module and a depthwise convolution module between two half-step feed-forward layers; an RNN-T decoder emits tokens.
table:
| Model | WER test-clean (%) | WER test-other (%) |
| Conformer-L (ours) | 2.1 | 4.3 |
| Transformer transducer | 2.4 | 5.6 |
| LSTM encoder | 3.2 | 7.9 |
conclusion: Convolution-augmented attention is the strongest ASR encoder we tested.

title: Self-Supervised Speech Representations from Masked Prediction
abstract: Masked prediction of discovered acoustic units learns speech representations from unlabeled audio. Fine-tuned with only ten hours of labels, the model rivals fully supervised speech recognition.
method: K-means clusters of MFCC features provide the first targets; later iterations re-cluster the model's own hidden states. Fine-tuning uses CTC loss.
table:
| Labeled data | WER test-clean (%) | WER test-other (%) |
| 10 hours (ours) | 4.3 | 9.4 |
| 100 hours (ours) | 2.9 | 6.8 |
| 100 hours supervised | 6.1 | 17.1 |
conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining makes low-resource speech recognition practical.

title: Streaming Speech Recognition with Chunked Attention
abstract: On-device assistants need speech recognition that emits words while the user speaks. Chunked attention limits look-ahead to a fixed window and trades a little accuracy for low latency.
method: The encoder attends within fixed 640 ms chunks plus a cached left context; a two-pass rescoring step with full context fixes errors at the end of the utterance.
table:
| Model | WER (%) | Latency (ms) |
| Chunked attention (ours) | 5.8 | 320 |
| Full-context attention | 5.1 | 2400 |
| Streaming LSTM | 7.4 | 290 |
conclusion: Chunked attention keeps streaming ASR within 0.7 points of full context.

title: Multilingual Speech Recognition with a Shared Subword Vocabulary
abstract: A single acoustic model trained on 51 languages with a shared subword vocabulary helps low-resource languages most. We report word error rate on the FLEURS benchmark.
method: Language-adaptive layer norms and a shared 16k sentencepiece vocabulary let the encoder share phonetic structure across languages.
table:
| Model | Avg WER FLEURS (%) | Languages |
| Shared vocabulary (ours) | 11.8 | 51 |
| Monolingual models | 17.5 | 51 |
| Per-language vocabulary | 13.9 | 51 |
conclusion: Sharing subwords across languages transfers acoustic knowledge to low-resource speech.

title: Noise-Robust Speech Recognition via Data Augmentation
abstract: Spectrogram masking and simulated room impulse responses make speech recognition robust to noisy far-field audio without any architectural change.
method: Time and frequency masks are applied to log-mel spectrograms; clean utterances are convolved with simulated rooms and mixed with noise at 0 to 20 dB SNR.
table:
| Training data | WER CHiME-4 (%) | WER clean (%) |
| Augmented (ours) | 9.7 | 3.9 |
| Clean only | 21.3 | 3.6 |
| Multi-condition recordings | 11.2 | 4.0 |
conclusion: Cheap augmentation closes most of the gap to recorded multi-condition data.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Open-Domain Question Answering
abstract: We combine a dense passage retriever with a sequence-to-sequence generator and train them end to end, so the generator conditions on retrieved Wikipedia passages when answering open-domain questions.
method: The retriever's top-k passages are marginalised over during generation; the retriever's query encoder is updated through the generation loss.
table:
| Model | Natural Questions EM | TriviaQA EM |
| RAG (ours) | 44.5 | 56.8 |
| Closed-book T5 | 34.5 | 50.1 |
| Extractive DPR reader | 41.5 | 57.9 |
conclusion: Retrieval-augmented generation beats closed-book models of the same size.

title: Dense Passage Retrieval with Hard Negatives for Question Answering
abstract: A dual encoder trained with in-batch and BM25 hard negatives retrieves passages that contain the answer far more often than sparse retrieval, which improves the downstream question answering reader.
method: Questions and passages are encoded by separate BERT encoders; similarity is the dot product, and an approximate nearest neighbour index serves 21 million passages.
table:
| Retriever | Top-20 accuracy NQ (%) | Top-100 accuracy NQ (%) |
| DPR (ours) | 78.4 | 85.4 |
| BM25 | 59.1 | 73.7 |
| BM25 + DPR | 76.6 | 83.8 |
conclusion: Learned dense retrieval is a better first stage for question answering than BM25.

title: Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
abstract: A retrieval-augmented language model that decides when to retrieve and critiques its own generations with reflection tokens improves factuality on long-form question answering.
method: Special reflection tokens predict whether retrieval is needed and whether each retrieved passage supports the continuation; decoding uses these tokens to rank segments.
table:
| Model | PopQA accuracy | Biography FactScore |
| Self-reflective RAG (ours) | 54.9 | 81.2 |
| Standard RAG | 52.8 | 71.6 |
| No retrieval | 29.3 | 63.4 |
conclusion: Letting the model control retrieval improves factual precision of long answers.

title: Multi-Hop Question Answering with Iterative Retrieval
abstract: Multi-hop questions need evidence that is only findable after the first hop is read. Iterative retrieval interleaves reasoning steps with new queries built from the partial chain of thought.
method: After each generated reasoning sentence the model issues a new retrieval query; retrieved paragraphs are appended to the context for the next step.
table:
| Method | HotpotQA F1 | 2WikiMultiHop F1 |
| Iterative retrieval (ours) | 61.2 | 58.7 |
| One-step retrieval | 49.8 | 43.1 |
| No retrieval | 38.4 | 32.9 |
conclusion: Interleaving retrieval with reasoning is key for multi-hop question answering.

title: Evaluating Faithfulness of Retrieval-Augmented Answers
abstract: Retrieval-augmented systems often produce fluent answers that their retrieved context does not support. We release a benchmark of human faithfulness judgments and an automatic metric that correlates with them.
method: Answers are split into atomic claims; an entailment model checks each claim against the retrieved passages and the score is the supported fraction.
table:
| Metric | Spearman with humans | Cost per 1k answers (USD) |
| Claim entailment (ours) | 0.71 | 2.40 |
| ROUGE-L | 0.18 | 0.01 |
| LLM judge | 0.64 | 18.00 |
conclusion: Claim-level entailment is a cheap and reliable faithfulness metric for RAG.

title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
abstract: We train a five-finger robot hand to reorient objects in hand with model-free reinforcement learning, using demonstrations and an off-policy critic to reach high success with few real-world episodes.
method: Soft actor-critic is initialised from 50 teleoperated demonstrations; a learned reward classifier replaces hand-designed rewards on the real robot.
table:
| Method | Success rate (%) | Real-world episodes |
| SAC + demos (ours) | 86 | 400 |
| SAC from scratch | 31 | 400 |
| Behaviour cloning | 52 | 0 |
conclusion: Demonstrations plus off-policy RL make dexterous manipulation trainable on hardware.

title: Sim-to-Real Transfer of Grasping Policies with Domain Randomization
abstract: Policies trained only in simulation with randomised textures, lighting and dynamics transfer to a real robot arm for bin picking without any real training data.
method: PPO trains a vision-based grasping policy across 100k randomised simulated scenes; camera pose and friction coefficients are sampled per episode.
table:
| Policy | Real grasp success (%) | Unseen objects success (%) |
| Randomized sim (ours) | 91.3 | 84.0 |
| Fixed sim | 38.5 | 22.1 |
| Real-data supervised | 89.7 | 76.4 |
conclusion: Enough randomization makes simulation a substitute for real robot data.

title: Offline Reinforcement Learning from Robot Play Data
abstract: Unstructured play data collected by teleoperators covers many behaviours. Offline reinforcement learning with goal relabelling turns it into a goal-conditioned manipulation policy for a kitchen robot.
method: Implicit Q-learning is trained on relabelled goals from 7 hours of play; the policy conditions on goal images.
table:
| Method | Kitchen task success (%) | Tasks |
| Offline IQL (ours) | 73.5 | 12 |
| Goal-conditioned BC | 48.2 | 12 |
| Online RL | 21.0 | 12 |
conclusion: Offline RL extracts reusable skills from cheap robot play data.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robot Assembly
abstract: Assembling furniture needs dozens of steps. A high-level policy chooses skills and a low-level reinforcement learning controller executes them, so the robot completes long-horizon assembly tasks.
method: The manager selects among learned skills every 50 control steps; skills are trained with dense rewards and the manager with sparse task completion reward.
table:
| Method | Assembly completion (%) | Avg steps |
| Hierarchical RL (ours) | 67.0 | 412 |
| Flat PPO | 9.5 | 1000 |
| Scripted skills | 44.0 | 530 |
conclusion: Skill hierarchies make long-horizon robot manipulation tractable for RL.

title: Reward Learning from Human Preferences for Robot Manipulation
abstract: Writing reward functions for manipulation is error prone. We learn the reward from pairwise human preferences over short robot clips and optimise it with reinforcement learning.
method: A Bradley-Terry reward model is fit to 1500 preference queries; PPO optimises the learned reward and new queries are chosen by ensemble disagreement.
table:
| Reward | Task success (%) | Human queries |
| Preference reward (ours) | 82.0 | 1500 |
| Hand-designed reward | 70.5 | 0 |
| Random queries | 64.0 | 1500 |
conclusion: Preference-based rewards beat hand-written ones with modest human effort.

title: Feature Pyramid Networks for Object Detection
abstract: A top-down pathway with lateral connections builds a feature pyramid with strong semantics at every scale, improving object detection of small objects on COCO.
method: Each pyramid level merges the upsampled coarser map with the corresponding backbone map; region proposals and the detection head run on all levels.
table:
| Detector | COCO box AP | AP small |
| Faster R-CNN + FPN (ours) | 36.2 | 18.2 |
| Faster R-CNN C4 | 31.6 | 13.5 |
| SSD512 | 28.8 | 10.9 |
conclusion: Feature pyramids are a cheap and general improvement for object detectors.

title: End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers and Set Prediction
abstract: We treat object detection as direct set prediction with a transformer decoder and bipartite matching, which removes anchors and non-maximum suppression from the detection pipeline.
method: A fixed set of 100 learned object queries attends to CNN features; the Hungarian algorithm matches predictions to ground truth boxes for the loss.
table:
| Detector | COCO box AP | Epochs |
| Transformer detector (ours) | 42.0 | 500 |
| Faster R-CNN + FPN | 42.0 | 109 |
| Deformable variant (ours) | 46.2 | 50 |
conclusion: Set prediction simplifies detection; deformable attention fixes slow convergence.

title: Anchor-Free One-Stage Object Detection with Center Sampling
abstract: Predicting boxes as distances from object centres removes anchor boxes and their hyper-parameters. Our anchor-free one-stage detector is faster and more accurate than anchor-based peers on COCO.
method: Locations inside a centre region of each object are positives; a centre-ness branch down-weights low-quality boxes far from the centre.
table:
| Detector | COCO box AP | FPS |
| Anchor-free (ours) | 44.7 | 26 |
| RetinaNet | 40.8 | 19 |
| YOLOv3 | 33.0 | 45 |
conclusion: Anchor-free detection is simpler and stronger than anchor-based one-stage detection.

title: Open-Vocabulary Object Detection with Vision-Language Pretraining
abstract: A detector whose classifier is replaced by text embeddings of category names detects categories never seen with box labels. We distill region embeddings from a vision-language model.
method: Region features are aligned to CLIP image embeddings of cropped proposals; at test time any category name is embedded by the text encoder.
table:
| Detector | LVIS AP rare | COCO novel AP50 |
| Open-vocabulary (ours) | 25.6 | 36.6 |
| Supervised on base classes | 9.4 | 1.3 |
| Captions only | 18.1 | 27.0 |
conclusion: Vision-language distillation unlocks open-vocabulary object detection.

title: Real-Time Object Detection on Edge Devices
abstract: We design a detector for mobile chips by searching backbone widths under a latency budget and quantising to 8-bit integers, keeping COCO accuracy close to server models.
method: Neural architecture search scores candidate networks with measured on-device latency; quantisation-aware training recovers accuracy lost to int8.
table:
| Detector | COCO box AP | Latency on phone (ms) |
| Edge detector (ours) | 34.1 | 11.2 |
| MobileNetV2-SSDLite | 22.1 | 14.5 |
| Server detector | 41.0 | 210.0 |
conclusion: Latency-aware search plus int8 quantisation gives real-time detection on phones.

title: Diffusion Policies for Visuomotor Robot Manipulation
abstract: We represent a robot's visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process over action sequences, which handles multimodal demonstrations better than regression policies.
method: A diffusion model denoises a 16-step action chunk conditioned on camera images; receding-horizon control executes the first 8 actions.
table:
| Policy | Push-T success (%) | Real pouring success (%) |
| Diffusion policy (ours) | 91.0 | 79.0 |
| LSTM-GMM | 67.0 | 40.0 |
| Implicit BC | 69.0 | 35.0 |
conclusion: Diffusion models are an expressive policy class for robot manipulation.

title: Contextual Biasing of Speech Recognition with Retrieved Entity Lists
abstract: Rare names are the most common speech recognition errors in assistants. We retrieve a short list of likely entities for each utterance and bias the decoder toward them.
method: A retriever selects 50 entity names from a catalogue using the first-pass hypothesis; a cross-attention biasing module reads them during second-pass decoding.
table:
| System | Overall WER (%) | Entity WER (%) |
| Retrieved biasing (ours) | 6.2 | 14.8 |
| No biasing | 6.5 | 31.6 |
| Full catalogue biasing | 7.9 | 18.3 |
conclusion: Retrieval keeps contextual biasing lists short and accurate.

title: Synthetic Training Data from Diffusion Models for Object Detection
abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate labelled training scenes. We paste generated objects into backgrounds and train detectors for rare categories where real boxes are scarce.
method: A diffusion model generates object crops from category prompts; a segmentation model extracts masks and copy-paste builds detection images with boxes.
table:
| Training data | LVIS AP rare | COCO box AP |
| Real + synthetic (ours) | 21.4 | 44.9 |
| Real only | 15.2 | 44.6 |
| Synthetic only | 9.8 | 27.3 |
conclusion: Diffusion-generated data mostly helps rare categories in object detection.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Language Models for Molecular Property Questions
abstract: Chemistry questions about specific molecules need facts from the literature. A retrieval-augmented language model answers property questions by retrieving passages about the queried molecule.
method: Molecule names and SMILES strings are normalised before dense retrieval over 2 million chemistry abstracts; the generator cites retrieved passages.
table:
| Model | ChemQA accuracy (%) | Citation precision (%) |
| Retrieval-augmented (ours) | 68.3 | 81.0 |
| Closed-book LLM | 47.9 | - |
| Graph neural network baseline | 52.6 | - |
conclusion: Retrieval grounds chemistry answers that closed-book models hallucinate.

title: Object Detection for Robotic Grasp Planning in Clutter
abstract: A robot clearing a cluttered bin first detects objects, then plans grasps per detection. We study how detector accuracy limits grasp success.
method: A Mask R-CNN detector proposes object masks; a grasp quality network ranks antipodal grasps inside each mask; no reinforcement learning is used.
table:
| Detector | Mask AP | Grasp success (%) |
| Fine-tuned Mask R-CNN (ours) | 71.2 | 88.5 |
| COCO-pretrained only | 48.9 | 70.1 |
| No detector (whole-bin grasps) | - | 61.4 |
conclusion: Better detection directly raises grasp success in clutter.

title: Spoken Question Answering over Retrieved Lecture Transcripts
abstract: Students ask spoken questions about recorded lectures. We transcribe lectures with speech recognition, retrieve transcript segments for each question and answer from them.
method: An ASR system transcribes lectures; questions are transcribed too, and a dense retriever selects transcript windows that a reader model answers from.
table:
| System | Answer F1 | Transcript WER (%) |
| Retrieve-then-read (ours) | 58.4 | 12.1 |
| Read whole transcript | 41.0 | 12.1 |
| Gold transcripts | 66.9 | 0.0 |
conclusion: Retrieval over noisy ASR transcripts makes lecture question answering feasible.

title: Learned Index Structures for Range Queries
abstract: A hierarchy of small regression models can replace a B-tree by predicting the position of a key in a sorted array, using less memory for range queries.
method: A root model routes keys to leaf linear models; a bounded binary search corrects the predicted position within the model's maximum error.
table:
| Index | Lookup time (ns) | Size (MB) |
| Learned index (ours) | 98 | 0.15 |
| B-tree | 260 | 12.8 |
| Hash map | 70 | 64.0 |
conclusion: Learned models are a compact alternative to B-trees for read-heavy workloads.

title: Autotuning Compiler Loop Schedules with Cost Models
abstract: Choosing tile sizes and loop orders for tensor programs is a huge search problem. A learned cost model ranks candidate schedules so that only the best few are compiled and measured.
method: Programs are featurised from their loop nests; a gradient boosted tree predicts throughput and an evolutionary search proposes schedules.
table:
| Approach | Speedup over vendor library | Tuning time (min) |
| Cost-model search (ours) | 1.32 | 45 |
| Random search | 1.05 | 240 |
| Hand-written schedules | 1.00 | - |
conclusion: Learned cost models make schedule autotuning fast enough for everyday use.

title: Statistical Downscaling of Precipitation Forecasts
abstract: Global forecasts are too coarse for local flood warnings. We downscale precipitation from 25 km to 2.5 km grids with quantile regression on terrain features.
method: Quantile regression forests map coarse forecast fields and elevation, slope and aspect to local precipitation quantiles.
table:
| Method | CRPS (mm) | Brier score heavy rain |
| Quantile forest (ours) | 0.84 | 0.061 |
| Bilinear interpolation | 1.27 | 0.094 |
| Linear regression | 1.02 | 0.079 |
conclusion: Terrain-aware statistical downscaling sharpens local precipitation forecasts.

title: Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Novel View Synthesis
abstract: Representing a scene as millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians allows differentiable rasterisation at real-time frame rates while matching the quality of neural radiance fields.
method: Gaussians are initialised from structure-from-motion points and optimised with adaptive densification; a tile-based rasteriser sorts them per pixel.
table:
| Method | PSNR Mip-NeRF360 (dB) | FPS |
| Gaussian splatting (ours) | 27.21 | 134 |
| Mip-NeRF360 | 27.69 | 0.06 |
| Instant-NGP | 25.59 | 9.4 |
conclusion: Explicit Gaussians bring radiance-field quality to real-time rendering.
